newsitem.title: USA: Talks start on Korea peace proposals.
newsitem.headline: Talks start on Korea peace proposals.

text.p: South Korean, North Korean and U.S. officials on Wednesday sat down at the same table for the first time to begin discussing proposals for international talks on ending the technical state of war on the Korean peninsula.

Witnesses said the meeting began with members of the delegations shaking hands, exchanging small talk and pleasantries. The three heads of delegation then clasped their hands together, one on top of the other.

"The atmosphere was pleasant, they were all very pleasant with another," said New York Foreign Press Centre spokesman Kenneth Bailes, who observed the start of the meeting in a conference room in Manhattan's Hilton Hotel.

The meeting was held during a period of high tension between bitter rivals North and South Korea, including a string of defections from the North and reports of famine and economic collapse in the Stalinist state long allied with China and the former Soviet Union.

Wednesday's meeting stemmed from last April's proposal to North Korea by President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam for four-way talks, including China, to work out a peace agreement to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
The United States fought alongside South Korea during the war, while China supported North Korea.

The meeting, described by the U.S. State Department as a "joint briefing," was convened at the request of Pyongyang, which wanted more information on Washington and Seoul's proposals for such talks. Actual negotiations may not start until July or so, a senior U.S. official said on Monday.

It was the first time officials from Pyongyang and Seoul have met to discuss armistice issues, although their representatives have met on other topics, most notably over an international agreement to freeze North Korea's nuclear programme.

A reporter allowed into the room for a brief photo opportunity said the South Korean delegation head, deputy minister for political affairs Song Young Shik, told North Korean counterpart Kim Gye Gwan "this is a significant event," to which Kim apparently indicated agreement. Kim is vice minister for foreign affairs.
The United States delegation is headed by Charles Kartman, U.S. deputy assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs.
Delegations were seated at circular tables for the meeting, which could last all day, depending on how the North Koreans respond to the U.S. and South Korean proposals, U.S. officials said.

"There is one round table and then there are three secondary tables ... they're in a circular arrangement and the heads of the delegation are seated at the table and the junior members are seated at the small tables behind," Bailes told reporters.
A senior U.S. official privy to the discussions said on Monday that the shape of the table was a "big deal" that was negotiated, along with some related issues, over the course of several days.

Laborious negotiations on table shape and seating arrangements also accompanied such momentous negotiations as the Paris peace talks to end the Vietnam War and the 1991 Madrid peace conference that launched direct peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians, Syria and Lebanon.
North Korea has twice delayed taking part in the New York talks in what was seen as an effort to press Washington to provide more food aid to its famine-stricken people.
North Korea had been demanding that the armistice be scrapped to pave the way for a peace treaty, but solely with the United States, something unacceptable to South Korea.
